metric_definition.name: New-user 7-day Return Rate
metric_definition.new_user: A user on the date of their first_visit event.
metric_definition.eligible_cohort: first_visit_date <= 2021-01-24, allowing a complete seven-day observation window.
metric_definition.returned_within_7_days: At least one session_start on day 1 through day 7 after first_visit; same-day sessions are excluded.

data_quality.auxiliary_event_warning: add_to_cart had 18 zero-volume days between 2020-11-02 and 2020-11-24. This does not affect the return-rate definition. The recommended baseline begins after the anomaly, so first-session activation comparisons use a clean interval.

candidate_decline.pattern: Return rate declined across multiple consecutive weekly cohorts, reached 5.27% and 4.94% in the two target weeks, then partially recovered in January.
candidate_decline.materiality: The recommended target is 3.22 percentage points below the conservative baseline, a 38.61% relative decline.
candidate_decline.statistical_check: Approximate 95% confidence interval for target minus baseline: -3.56 to -2.87 percentage points.

recommended_windows.selection_rationale: Both windows contain two complete natural cohort weeks with full seven-day observation. The baseline begins after the add_to_cart collection anomaly and includes the already-weaker 2020-12-07 cohort, making the comparison conservative. The target contains two consecutive low weeks rather than one isolated minimum; 2020-12-14 is retained as a transition week.

initial_segment_findings.interpretation: The decline is broad across acquisition and device rather than localized to one large segment. Deeper first-session activation remains associated with higher return rates in both periods, while the reached-view-item segment shows the largest observed decline. These are descriptive associations, not causal findings.

evidence: The two target cohorts contain 33,313 eligible new users and 1,703 seven-day returners.
Target return rate was 5.11% versus 8.33% in the conservative baseline, a -3.22 percentage-point change.
Both target weeks were low (5.27% and 4.94%), so the finding is not based on a single day or week.
first_visit and session_start were present on all 92 dates, with no primary-event collection break detected.
Declines appeared across all material acquisition and device segments examined.
hypotheses: Holiday-period intent or seasonality may contribute to lower return behavior.
A change in new-user engagement quality may be associated with the decline, given weaker return rates among users who reached view_item as well as shallow users.
Broad changes affecting multiple traffic sources and devices may be more plausible than a single-channel or single-device issue.
unknowns: Whether the decline reflects holiday seasonality, campaign mix, merchandising, pricing, UX, or another external factor.
Whether source values obfuscated as <Other> conceal meaningful acquisition changes.
Whether consent, identity, or tracking changes altered cross-session user recognition without creating a visible event-volume break.
Whether the same pattern persists under longer return windows or year-over-year controls.
productization_assessment: Strong enough to productize as a bounded Lifecycle Risk case: the decline is material, sustained across two target cohorts, statistically clear, and based on large, fully observed cohorts. The product must preserve evidence discipline: this is a detected and segmented risk, not a causal root cause, and holiday seasonality remains an important unknown.
